newsitem.title: USA: Futures funds seen benefiting from stock profits.
newsitem.headline: Futures funds seen benefiting from stock profits.

text.p: More cash may flow into managed futures funds and other alternative investments in 1997, as some investors begin to shift profits out of U.S. stocks, several futures funds analysts said.

"The stock market has had one of the greatest runs in history and we are starting to see some investors taking profits and reinvesting them into managed futures," said Sol Waksman, president of Barclays Trading Group LLC of Fairfield, Iowa.
Managed futures funds invest in futures and options in both financial and commodity markets.

According to Barclays, about $21.5 billion in assets were held by 500 managed futures funds through most of 1996, and Waksman and other analysts see the amount increasing if some investors continue to take profits from stocks.

"We aren't seeing clients reduce exposure in stocks, but we are seeing them put profits into managed futures," said Richard Bornhoft, president of Hart-Bornhoft Inc which tracks the performance of 1,000 futures funds.
While assets in the 500 managed futures funds tracked by Barclays have grown from $10.5 billion in 1990, total assets so for 1996 still remain below the peak of $26 billion in 1993.

The Managed Futures Association at its annual three-day conference in Palm Beach, Florida, starting Sunday hopes to discuss ways in which to educate the public, currently enamored of U.S. mutual funds, about investing in managed futures.
In recent years, the MFA has faced the public's concerns about managed futures due to several debacles at banks and companies involving the use of derivatives.

"As a general rule, the industry must try to get innovative in terms of making alternative investments and managed futures more appealing to investors," Ken Tropin, president of Graham Capital Management and former MFA chairman, said.
Managed futures funds and hedge funds are not correlated to stock and bond prices, and use futures and options as part of various strategies to profit under a wide variety of economic environments.
While these funds, on average, have produced sizable returns, those returns have paled compared to the stock market's gains in the last two years, Waksman said.

Lois Peltz, managing editor of Managed Accounts Report Inc, said its index monitoring the performance of commodity trading advisers (CTAs) was up 14.6 percent in 1996, versus up 15 percent in 1995. CTAs advise the buying and selling of futures contracts or commodity options and must be registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Hedge Fund Research Inc, which tracks 2,500 hedge funds worldwide with a total of $200 billion in assets, said its main index was up 20.22 percent in 1996. ((Derivatives desk 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuters.com))
